decks.title: Circles: Angle Properties — Part 1: Angle at the centre, same segment and semicircle
goals: State and prove that the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference
Use equal chords and equal arcs with the angles they subtend at the centre
Use angles in the same segment to transfer an angle across a circle figure
Prove and use the fact that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle

slides.heading: Circles: angles, Part 1
slides.body_md: An arc of a circle looks **twice as wide** from the centre as it does from the rim. In this part we prove that, and use it together with two companion facts to find angles.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O. The arc AB at the bottom is joined to the centre O and to a point P on the opposite part of the circle. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees and the angle APB at the point P is 50 degrees, half as large.
visual.caption: The arc $AB$ looks twice as wide from the centre ($100^\circ$) as from the rim ($50^\circ$).

slides.narration: Welcome to circles and angles. This arc is seen from two places: the centre, and a point on the rim. From the centre it looks twice as wide as from the rim. Here the angle at the centre is one hundred degrees and the angle at the rim is fifty. In this part we prove that fact, and use it with the same segment property and the semicircle property.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: State and prove the **centre and circumference** theorem
Use **equal chords** and equal arcs
Use **angles in the same segment**
Prove and use the **angle in a semicircle**

rows: double the angle at any point of the remaining circumference
opposite angles supplementary; exterior angle equals interior opposite

visual.alt: Table of the circle properties in this chapter: the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference; equal chords and arcs give equal angles at the centre; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is a right angle; cyclic quadrilaterals are covered in part 2.
visual.caption: Five properties; part 1 covers the first four.

slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. We prove the theorem about the angle at the centre. We use equal chords and equal arcs. We use angles in the same segment, and we prove that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle. Part two then moves on to cyclic quadrilaterals.

slides.heading: Words about a circle
slides.body_md: A **chord** joins two points of the circle; a chord through the centre is a **diameter**. A chord cuts the circle into a **minor arc** and a **major arc**. An arc **subtends** an angle at a point when its ends are joined to that point.
bullets: the two parts cut off by a chord are the **segments**
a point on the **major arc** and the centre look at the minor arc

visual.alt: A circle with centre O. A diameter AB passes through O, a chord PQ lies above it near the top, and a radius OR runs from O to the lower right of the circle.
visual.caption: Diameter $AB$, chord $PQ$ and radius $OR$. The chord $PQ$ cuts the circle into a minor arc and a major arc.

slides.narration: Here are the words we need. A chord joins two points of the circle. A chord through the centre is a diameter. Every chord cuts the circle into a shorter arc, called the minor arc, and a longer one, called the major arc. An arc subtends an angle at a point when the two ends of the arc are joined to that point.

slides.heading: The angle at the centre is double
slides.body_md: The angle subtended by an arc at the **centre** is **double** the angle it subtends at any point on the **remaining part** of the circle.
bullets: same arc $AB$ for both angles
here $80^\circ = 2 \times 40^\circ$

visual.alt: A circle with centre O, an arc AB at the bottom subtending 80 degrees at the centre, and a point C on the major arc from which the same arc subtends 40 degrees.
visual.caption: $\angle AOB = 80^\circ = 2 \times \angle ACB = 2 \times 40^\circ$.

slides.narration: Here is the first theorem. The angle that an arc makes at the centre is double the angle it makes at any point on the remaining part of the circle. In the picture, the arc subtends eighty degrees at the centre and forty degrees at the point C on the rim. Eighty is twice forty, and the same holds for every point on the major arc.

slides.heading: Proof of the theorem
slides.body_md: Let $P$ be a point on the major arc with $O$ inside $\angle APB$. Join $PO$ and produce it to $Q$; put $\angle OPA = x$ and $\angle OPB = y$.
bullets: $OP = OA$, so $\angle OAP = x$; the exterior angle $\angle AOQ = x + x = 2x$
in the same way $\angle BOQ = 2y$
adding: $\angle AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y) = 2\angle APB$

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and a point P at the top. The line PO is produced to meet the circle again at Q at the bottom. A and B are points on either side, joined to O and to P. The angle OPA is marked x with one arc and the angle OPB is marked y with two arcs.
visual.caption: Join $PO$ and produce it to $Q$. Then $\angle AOQ = 2x$ and $\angle BOQ = 2y$, so $\angle AOB = 2(x + y)$.

slides.narration: To prove it, join P to O and extend to Q. Call the angle O P A by the name x and the angle O P B by the name y. The radii O P and O A are equal, so the angle at A is also x, and the exterior angle A O Q is two x. In the same way B O Q is two y. Adding, the angle A O B is two x plus two y, which is twice the angle A P B.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from the centre to the rim
slides.body_md: The arc $AB$ subtends $\angle AOB = 110^\circ$ at the centre $O$. Find $\angle ACB$, where $C$ is on the major arc.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the angle at the circumference is **half** the angle at the centre
**Step 2 —** $\angle ACB = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 110^\circ = 55^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 1: a circle with centre O. The angle AOB at the centre is 110 degrees and the angle ACB at a point C on the major arc is to be found.
visual.caption: Given $\angle AOB = 110^\circ$; find $\angle ACB$.

slides.narration: The angle at the centre is one hundred and ten degrees. The angle at the circumference on the same arc is half of that. Half of one hundred and ten degrees is fifty five degrees, so the angle at C is fifty five degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: centre and rim
slides.body_md: Which is the right comparison?
slides.narration: Which statement compares the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference on the same arc? Remember which one is double.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: rim to centre, then an isosceles triangle
slides.body_md: A point $P$ on the major arc sees the chord $AB$ under $\angle APB = 38^\circ$. Find $\angle AOB$ and then $\angle OAB$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle AOB = 2 \times 38^\circ = 76^\circ$
**Step 2 —** $OA = OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles with equal base angles
**Step 3 —** $\angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 76^\circ}{2} = 52^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 2: a circle with centre O. A point P on the major arc sees the chord AB under an angle of 38 degrees. The angle AOB at the centre and the base angle OAB of the triangle OAB are marked with question marks.
visual.caption: Given $\angle APB = 38^\circ$; find $\angle AOB$ and then $\angle OAB$.

slides.narration: Now we go the other way. The angle at the rim is thirty eight degrees, so the angle at the centre is double, seventy six degrees. Then the triangle O A B has two equal sides, the radii, so its base angles are equal. Each base angle is one hundred and eighty minus seventy six, all over two, which is fifty two degrees.

slides.heading: A point on the minor arc
slides.body_md: If the point is on the **minor** arc $AB$, it looks at the **major** arc, whose angle at the centre is the **reflex** angle $360^\circ - \angle AOB$.
bullets: here $\angle AOB = 100^\circ$ and $\angle AQB = \dfrac{360^\circ - 100^\circ}{2} = 130^\circ$
the angles from the two sides of a chord add up to $180^\circ$

visual.alt: A circle with centre O. The chord AB near the bottom subtends 100 degrees at the centre. A point Q on the minor arc AB, between A and B, sees the chord under 130 degrees, half of the reflex angle 260 degrees.
visual.caption: From $Q$ on the minor arc the angle is $130^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (360^\circ - 100^\circ)$.

slides.narration: What if the point is on the short arc? Then it looks at the long arc, which makes a reflex angle at the centre. Three hundred and sixty minus one hundred is two hundred and sixty, and half of that is one hundred and thirty degrees. Notice that fifty and one hundred and thirty add up to one hundred and eighty, the angles from the two sides of the chord.

slides.heading: Equal chords and equal arcs
slides.body_md: **Equal chords** of a circle subtend **equal angles at the centre**, and so do **equal arcs**. Conversely, equal angles at the centre give equal chords.
bullets: equal arcs have equal chords
equal angles at the rim stand on equal chords as well

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and two equal chords AB and CD, marked with one tick each. Each chord is joined to the centre, and the angles AOB and COD at the centre are both 70 degrees.
visual.caption: Equal chords $AB = CD$ subtend equal angles ($70^\circ$) at the centre.

slides.narration: Equal chords of a circle make equal angles at the centre. The same is true of equal arcs. In this picture the chords A B and C D carry the same tick mark, so they are equal, and both subtend seventy degrees at the centre. The reverse also holds: equal angles at the centre mean equal chords.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: equal chords
slides.body_md: Chords $AB$ and $BC$ are equal and $\angle AOB = 64^\circ$. $D$ is on the major arc $AC$. Find $\angle BOC$, $\angle AOC$, $\angle ADC$ and $\angle ABC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** equal chords: $\angle BOC = \angle AOB = 64^\circ$
**Step 2 —** $\angle AOC = 64^\circ + 64^\circ = 128^\circ$
**Step 3 —** $\angle ADC = \dfrac{128^\circ}{2} = 64^\circ$
**Step 4 —** $B$ is on the minor arc $AC$: $\angle ABC = \dfrac{360^\circ - 128^\circ}{2} = 116^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 3: a circle with centre O and points A, B and C on the lower part, with equal chords AB and BC marked with ticks. D is a point on the major arc AC. The angle AOB is 64 degrees.
visual.caption: Chords $AB = BC$, $\angle AOB = 64^\circ$, $D$ on the major arc $AC$.

slides.narration: The chords A B and B C are equal, so they make equal angles at the centre, sixty four degrees each. Together the angle A O C is one hundred and twenty eight. The point D on the long arc sees it as half of that, sixty four degrees. The point B is on the short arc, so use the reflex angle: three hundred and sixty minus one hundred and twenty eight, halved, is one hundred and sixteen degrees.

slides.heading: Angles in the same segment
slides.body_md: Angles subtended by the **same chord** at points of the **same side** of it (the same segment) are **equal**.
bullets: points on the **opposite** side give the supplementary angle instead
all of them equal half the angle at the centre

visual.alt: A circle with a chord AB at the bottom and three points P, Q and R on the upper arc, all on the same side of AB. Each of the three points sees the chord AB under the same angle of 60 degrees.
visual.caption: Angles in the same segment are equal: $\angle APB = \angle AQB = \angle ARB = 60^\circ$.

slides.narration: Now the same segment property. Angles made by one chord at points on the same side of the chord are equal. Here three points on the upper arc all see the chord A B under sixty degrees. Points on the opposite side of the chord would see it under the supplementary angle, which is one hundred and twenty degrees. Every one of these equal angles is half the angle at the centre.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: chords that cross
slides.body_md: Chords $AC$ and $BD$ of a circle cut at $E$ inside it. $\angle ABD = 58^\circ$ and $\angle DAC = 35^\circ$. Find $\angle ACD$, $\angle DBC$ and $\angle ADC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle ACD = \angle ABD = 58^\circ$ (same segment of the chord $AD$)
**Step 2 —** $\angle DBC = \angle DAC = 35^\circ$ (same segment of the chord $DC$)
**Step 3 —** in $\triangle ADC$: $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 58^\circ = 87^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 4: a circle with four points A, B, C and D in order, joined to form a quadrilateral with both diagonals AC and BD drawn. The angle ABD is marked 58 degrees and the angle DAC is marked 35 degrees.
visual.caption: Chords $AC$ and $BD$; $\angle ABD = 58^\circ$, $\angle DAC = 35^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angles A B D and A C D stand on the same chord A D from the same side, so the angle at C is also fifty eight degrees. The angles D A C and D B C stand on the chord D C, so the angle at B is thirty five degrees. In the triangle A D C, the third angle is one hundred and eighty minus thirty five minus fifty eight, which is eighty seven degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: central angle of a track
slides.body_md: Half or double?
slides.narration: The central angle is given. Is the angle at a point on the major arc half of it, or double?

slides.heading: The angle in a semicircle
slides.body_md: The angle in a **semicircle** is a **right angle**: if $AB$ is a diameter and $P$ is any other point of the circle, then $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.
bullets: **Proof:** $OA = OP = OB$, so $\angle OAP = \angle OPA = x$ and $\angle OBP = \angle OPB = y$
in $\triangle ABP$: $x + y + (x + y) = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$
a special case of the centre theorem: the angle at the centre is $180^\circ$

visual.alt: A circle with a horizontal diameter AB through the centre O and a point P on the upper half. The angle APB is marked with a right-angle square. The radius OP is drawn, the angle OAP is marked x and the angle OBP is marked y.
visual.caption: Angle in a semicircle: $x + y + (x + y) = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle. To see why, join P to the centre. The radii are equal, so the two small triangles are isosceles, with base angles x on one side and y on the other. The three angles of the big triangle then add up to two x plus two y, which is one hundred and eighty degrees, so x plus y, the angle at P, is ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: two semicircle angles
slides.body_md: $AB$ is a diameter; $C$ and $D$ are points of the circle on opposite sides of $AB$, with $\angle CAB = 35^\circ$ and $\angle DBA = 28^\circ$. Find $\angle ABC$, $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CAD$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, so $\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$
**Step 2 —** $\angle ADB = 90^\circ$, so $\angle DAB = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ$
**Step 3 —** $C$ and $D$ are on opposite sides: $\angle CAD = 35^\circ + 62^\circ = 97^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 5: a circle with diameter AB. A point C above and a point D below the diameter are joined to A and B. The angle CAB is 35 degrees and the angle DBA is 28 degrees; the angles at C and D are marked as right angles.
visual.caption: Diameter $AB$; $\angle CAB = 35^\circ$, $\angle DBA = 28^\circ$; right angles at $C$ and $D$.

slides.narration: Because A B is a diameter, the angles at C and at D are both right angles. In the triangle A B C, the third angle is one hundred and eighty minus ninety minus thirty five, fifty five degrees. In the triangle A B D it is sixty two degrees. The points are on opposite sides of the diameter, so the angle C A D is thirty five plus sixty two, which is ninety seven degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a right angle in a semicircle
slides.body_md: Use the right angle first.
slides.narration: A diameter is given, so one angle of the triangle is ninety degrees. Use the angle sum to find the missing angle.

slides.heading: Which property should I use?
slides.body_md: Look at what is in the figure, then pick the property that matches. Many problems need **two or three** steps in a row.

nodes.label: An unknown angle in a circle figure: what do you see?
Centre involved: angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim
A diameter: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle
Two angles on one chord, same side: they are equal
Four points round the circle: opposite angles add up to 180 degrees

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a circle property: start from an unknown angle; if the centre is involved use double the angle at the circumference; if a diameter is involved use the right angle in a semicircle; if two angles stand on one chord on the same side they are equal; if four points lie round the circle opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
visual.caption: Match what you see in the figure to the property.

slides.narration: To choose a property, look at the figure. If the centre is involved, use the double angle theorem. If a diameter is involved, use the right angle in a semicircle. If two angles stand on one chord from the same side, they are equal. If four points lie round the circle, opposite angles add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, which is the subject of part two.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Centre angle $= 2 \times$ rim angle on the same arc
Point on the minor arc: use the reflex angle at the centre
Equal chords: equal angles at the centre
Same segment: equal angles
Semicircle: a right angle

rows: find the angle at the centre or at the rim
copy an angle to another chord
transfer an angle across the figure

visual.alt: Summary table for part 1: the angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim; for a point on the minor arc use half of the reflex angle; equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim on the same arc. For a point on the short arc, use the reflex angle. Equal chords give equal angles at the centre. Angles in the same segment are equal, and the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Name the property (1 mark):** write the reason beside each angle you find
**Working (1–2 marks):** show the halving, doubling or subtraction
**Answer with unit (1 mark):** degrees
**Mistake:** halving when you should double, or the other way round
**Mistake:** using the same-segment rule for points on opposite sides of the chord
**Habit:** mark each new angle on the figure as you find it
slides.narration: In the exam, write the property as a reason next to each angle you find. Show the halving, doubling or subtraction in your working. Common slips are halving when you should double, and using the same segment rule for points on opposite sides of a chord. Mark each new angle on the figure as you find it.

decks.title: Circles: Cyclic Properties — Part 2: Cyclic quadrilaterals
goals: Prove that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary
Use the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle
Combine circle properties with triangles and algebra to find angles
Use the converse to show that four points are concyclic

slides.heading: Circles: cyclic quadrilaterals, Part 2
slides.body_md: When all four corners of a quadrilateral lie on a circle, its **opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$**. In this part we prove that, use it, and use its converse to show that four points lie on a circle.

visual.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD with all four corners on a circle. The angles at A and C are 75 degrees and 105 degrees, and the angles at B and D are 78 degrees and 102 degrees. Each pair of opposite angles adds up to 180 degrees.
visual.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$: $75^\circ + 105^\circ = 180^\circ$ and $78^\circ + 102^\circ = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. This quadrilateral has all four corners on a circle. Look at its opposite angles: seventy five and one hundred and five add up to one hundred and eighty, and so do seventy eight and one hundred and two. In this part we prove that fact, use it to find angles, and use its converse to show that points lie on a circle.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Prove that **opposite angles** are supplementary
Use the **exterior angle** property
Combine circle facts with **triangles and algebra**
Use the **converse**: show that points are concyclic

rows: find a missing angle of a cyclic quadrilateral
find an angle without the supplement
supplementary opposite angles: the corners are concyclic
prove that four points lie on a circle

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees; the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle; if opposite angles are supplementary the four corners are concyclic; a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We prove that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and use the exterior angle property. We combine circle facts with triangles and algebra. Finally we use the converse to show that four points lie on one circle. The table shows the whole part on one card.

slides.heading: Cyclic quadrilaterals
slides.body_md: A quadrilateral is **cyclic** when all four vertices lie on one circle; the vertices are then **concyclic**. A circle through $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ is called the **circumcircle**.
bullets: not every quadrilateral is cyclic
rectangles and squares always are

visual.alt: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD drawn inside it so that all four corners A, B, C and D lie on the circle.
visual.caption: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral: its vertices are concyclic.

slides.narration: A quadrilateral is cyclic when all four of its corners lie on one circle. We say the corners are concyclic. Not every quadrilateral is cyclic, but rectangles and squares always are. What can we say about the angles of a cyclic quadrilateral? That is the next theorem.

slides.heading: Opposite angles are supplementary
slides.body_md: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are **supplementary**: they add up to $180^\circ$.
bullets: **Proof:** join $B$ and $D$ to the centre $O$; let $\angle BOD = x$ on the side of $C$
$\angle BAD = \dfrac{x}{2}$ and $\angle BCD = \dfrac{360^\circ - x}{2}$ (centre theorem, reflex angle)
adding: $\angle A + \angle C = \dfrac{x}{2} + 180^\circ - \dfrac{x}{2} = 180^\circ$

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The chord BD is joined to the centre. The angle BOD at the centre is 150 degrees, the angle BAD at A is 75 degrees, half of it, and the angle BCD at C is 105 degrees, half of the reflex angle 210 degrees.
visual.caption: $\angle BAD = \dfrac{1}{2}(150^\circ) = 75^\circ$ and $\angle BCD = \dfrac{1}{2}(360^\circ - 150^\circ) = 105^\circ$.

slides.narration: Join B and D to the centre, and call the angle at the centre x, on the side of C. By the centre theorem the angle at A is half of x. The angle at C looks at the other arc, whose central angle is three hundred and sixty minus x, so the angle at C is half of that. Add them: the halves of x cancel, leaving one hundred and eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: opposite angles
slides.body_md: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle DAB = 102^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 85^\circ$. Find $\angle BCD$ and $\angle ADC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $A$ and $C$ are opposite: $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 102^\circ = 78^\circ$
**Step 2 —** $B$ and $D$ are opposite: $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 85^\circ = 95^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 1: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The angle at A is 102 degrees and the angle at B is 85 degrees; the angles at C and D are marked with question marks.
visual.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$ with $\angle DAB = 102^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 85^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angles at A and C are opposite, so they add up to one hundred and eighty. Angle C is one hundred and eighty minus one hundred and two, seventy eight degrees. The angles at B and D are also opposite, so angle D is one hundred and eighty minus eighty five, ninety five degrees.

slides.heading: The exterior angle
slides.body_md: If one side of a cyclic quadrilateral is **produced**, the **exterior angle** equals the **interior opposite angle**.
bullets: $\angle DCE = 180^\circ - \angle BCD$ (straight line) $= \angle BAD$ (opposite angles)
the interior opposite angle is the one at the vertex not on that side

visual.alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with the side BC produced beyond C to a point E. The exterior angle DCE and the opposite interior angle BAD both carry one arc and measure 75 degrees.
visual.caption: Exterior angle $\angle DCE = 75^\circ$ = interior opposite angle $\angle BAD = 75^\circ$.

slides.narration: Now extend one side of the quadrilateral. The exterior angle is equal to the interior opposite angle. Here B C is extended to E, and the exterior angle D C E is seventy five degrees, the same as the interior angle B A D at the opposite corner. It follows at once from the straight line and the opposite angle property.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: exterior angle
slides.body_md: $ABCD$ is cyclic, $BC$ is produced to $E$, $\angle DCE = 74^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 84^\circ$. Find $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** exterior angle = interior opposite angle: $\angle BAD = \angle DCE = 74^\circ$
**Step 2 —** $B$ and $D$ are opposite: $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 84^\circ = 96^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 2: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with BC produced to E. The exterior angle DCE is 74 degrees and the angle ABC is 84 degrees; the angles BAD and ADC are marked with question marks.
visual.caption: Exterior angle $\angle DCE = 74^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 84^\circ$.

slides.narration: The exterior angle at C equals the interior opposite angle at A, so angle B A D is seventy four degrees. The angles at B and D are opposite, so angle A D C is one hundred and eighty minus eighty four, which is ninety six degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the property
slides.body_md: What do opposite angles do?
slides.narration: In a quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle, what is true of each pair of opposite angles?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: angles with algebra
slides.body_md: $ABCD$ is cyclic with $\angle A = (3x + 5)^\circ$, $\angle C = (2x - 15)^\circ$ and $\angle B = (2x + 9)^\circ$. Find $x$ and all four angles.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $A$ and $C$ are opposite: $(3x + 5)^\circ + (2x - 15)^\circ = 180^\circ \Rightarrow 5x - 10 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 38$
**Step 2 —** $\angle A = 3 \times 38 + 5 = 119$ and $\angle C = 2 \times 38 - 15 = 61$
**Step 3 —** $\angle B = 2 \times 38 + 9 = 85$ and $\angle D = 180 - 85 = 95$

visual.alt: Worked example 3: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The angle at A is marked 3x plus 5 degrees, the angle at C is marked 2x minus 15 degrees, the angle at B is marked 2x plus 9 degrees, and the angle at D is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$ with $\angle A = (3x + 5)^\circ$, $\angle B = (2x + 9)^\circ$, $\angle C = (2x - 15)^\circ$.

slides.narration: Opposite angles add up to one hundred and eighty, so three x plus five plus two x minus fifteen equals one hundred and eighty. That gives five x minus ten equals one hundred and eighty, so x is thirty eight. Then angle A is one hundred and nineteen, angle C is sixty one, angle B is eighty five, and angle D is one hundred and eighty minus eighty five, ninety five.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: same segment, then opposite angles
slides.body_md: $ABCD$ is cyclic with $\angle ADB = 40^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = 62^\circ$. Find $\angle ACB$, $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle ACB = \angle ADB = 40^\circ$ (same segment of the chord $AB$)
**Step 2 —** in $\triangle ABC$: $\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 62^\circ - 40^\circ = 78^\circ$
**Step 3 —** opposite angles: $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 78^\circ = 102^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 4: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with both diagonals drawn. The angle ADB is marked 40 degrees and the angle BAC is marked 62 degrees.
visual.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$; $\angle ADB = 40^\circ$, $\angle BAC = 62^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angle A C B stands on the same chord as the angle A D B, so it is also forty degrees. In the triangle A B C the third angle is one hundred and eighty minus sixty two minus forty, which is seventy eight. Then the angle at D is opposite to the angle at B, so it is one hundred and eighty minus seventy eight, one hundred and two degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing angle
slides.body_md: Opposite angles add to $180^\circ$.
slides.narration: One angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is given. Find the angle at the opposite vertex.

slides.heading: The converse: proving points concyclic
slides.body_md: If a quadrilateral has a pair of **opposite angles supplementary**, or an exterior angle equal to the interior opposite angle, then its four vertices are **concyclic**.
bullets: also: equal angles on the **same side** of a chord mean the points lie on a circle

visual.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD with a circle through its four corners. The angles at B and D are 88 degrees and 92 degrees, which add up to 180 degrees, so the corners lie on one circle.
visual.caption: If $\angle B + \angle D = 88^\circ + 92^\circ = 180^\circ$, the four corners lie on a circle.

math: \angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; A, B, C, D \text{ concyclic}
slides.narration: The converse works in the other direction. If a quadrilateral has a pair of opposite angles that add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, then its four corners lie on a circle. In the picture, eighty eight plus ninety two is one hundred and eighty. Equal angles on the same side of a chord also show that the points are concyclic.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: is it cyclic?
slides.body_md: Is a quadrilateral with angles $82^\circ$, $95^\circ$, $98^\circ$, $85^\circ$ in order cyclic? What about a rhombus with angles $70^\circ$ and $110^\circ$?
bullets: **First —** $82^\circ + 98^\circ = 180^\circ$ and $95^\circ + 85^\circ = 180^\circ$: **cyclic**
**Rhombus —** $70^\circ + 70^\circ = 140^\circ$ and $140^\circ \ne 180^\circ$: **not cyclic**

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5: the quadrilateral with angles 82, 95, 98 and 85 degrees has both pairs of opposite angles adding to 180 degrees, so it is cyclic; the rhombus with angles 70 and 110 degrees has opposite angles 70 and 70 adding to 140 degrees, so it is not cyclic.
visual.caption: Test each pair of opposite angles.

slides.narration: To test whether a quadrilateral is cyclic, add each pair of opposite angles. For the first one, eighty two plus ninety eight is one hundred and eighty, and ninety five plus eighty five is one hundred and eighty, so it is cyclic. For the rhombus, opposite angles are seventy and seventy, which add to only one hundred and forty, so it is not cyclic.

slides.heading: Special quadrilaterals
slides.body_md: A **parallelogram** inscribed in a circle is a **rectangle**: its opposite angles are equal and add up to $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$. Its diagonals are **diameters**.
bullets: a rhombus is cyclic only if it is a square
an isosceles trapezium is always cyclic

visual.alt: A rectangle ABCD inscribed in a circle. Its diagonals AC and BD are both diameters and cross at the centre O. All four angles of the rectangle are marked as right angles.
visual.caption: A parallelogram inscribed in a circle is a rectangle; its diagonals are diameters.

slides.narration: A parallelogram has equal opposite angles. If it is also cyclic, the opposite angles add up to one hundred and eighty, so each one is ninety degrees and the parallelogram is a rectangle. Its diagonals are then diameters of the circle. A rhombus can be cyclic only if it is a square, and an isosceles trapezium is always cyclic.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a diameter and a cyclic quadrilateral
slides.body_md: $AB$ is a diameter of the circle through $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ (in order). $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$ and $\angle CAD = 35^\circ$. Find $\angle BAC$, $\angle ADC$ and $\angle DAB$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$ (semicircle): $\angle BAC = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$
**Step 2 —** opposite angles: $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$
**Step 3 —** $\angle DAB = \angle DAC + \angle CAB = 30^\circ + 35^\circ = 65^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 6: a circle with diameter AB and a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD above it, with the diagonal AC drawn. The angle ABC is 60 degrees, the angle CAD is 35 degrees, and the angle ACB is marked as a right angle.
visual.caption: Diameter $AB$; $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$, $\angle CAD = 35^\circ$.

slides.narration: Because A B is a diameter, the angle at C is ninety degrees, so the angle B A C is one hundred and eighty minus ninety minus sixty, thirty degrees. The angle at D is opposite to the angle at B, so it is one hundred and eighty minus sixty, one hundred and twenty. Finally the angle D A B is thirty five plus thirty, sixty five degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: which shape is always cyclic?
slides.body_md: Think of opposite angles.
slides.narration: Which shape always has opposite angles that add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, whatever its measurements?

slides.heading: Choosing between the properties
slides.body_md: In a figure with a **cyclic quadrilateral**, ask three questions in turn.

nodes.label: An unknown angle in a circle figure: what do you see?
Centre involved: angle at the centre is double the angle at the rim
A diameter: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle
Two angles on one chord, same side: they are equal
Four points round the circle: opposite angles add up to 180 degrees

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a circle property: start from an unknown angle; if the centre is involved use double the angle at the circumference; if a diameter is involved use the right angle in a semicircle; if two angles stand on one chord on the same side they are equal; if four points lie round the circle opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
visual.caption: Match what you see in the figure to the property.

slides.narration: In a figure with a cyclic quadrilateral, ask three questions. Is there an exterior angle? Then it equals the interior opposite angle. Are there two angles on the same chord? Then they are equal. Is there a diameter or the centre? Then use the right angle or the double angle. After that, finish with triangles and straight lines.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: sides produced to meet
slides.body_md: $ABCD$ is cyclic. The sides $AB$ and $DC$ are produced beyond $B$ and $C$ to meet at $E$. $\angle ADC = 70^\circ$ and $\angle DAB = 75^\circ$. Find $\angle EBC$, $\angle ECB$ and $\angle BEC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** exterior angle at $B$ equals the interior opposite angle: $\angle EBC = \angle ADC = 70^\circ$
**Step 2 —** exterior angle at $C$: $\angle ECB = \angle DAB = 75^\circ$
**Step 3 —** in $\triangle EBC$: $\angle BEC = 180^\circ - 70^\circ - 75^\circ = 35^\circ$

visual.alt: Worked example 7: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD whose sides AB and DC are produced beyond B and C to meet at a point E. The angle ADC is marked 70 degrees and the angle DAB is marked 75 degrees.
visual.caption: Sides $AB$ and $DC$ produced meet at $E$; $\angle ADC = 70^\circ$, $\angle DAB = 75^\circ$.

slides.narration: Extend A B and D C until they meet at E. The exterior angle at B equals the interior opposite angle at D, so it is seventy degrees. The exterior angle at C equals the interior opposite angle at A, so it is seventy five degrees. In the triangle E B C the third angle is one hundred and eighty minus seventy minus seventy five, thirty five degrees.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles supplementary
Exterior angle = interior opposite angle
Converse: supplementary opposite angles mean concyclic
A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle
Combine with triangles, straight lines, same segment and semicircle

rows: find a missing angle of a cyclic quadrilateral
find an angle without the supplement
supplementary opposite angles: the corners are concyclic
prove that four points lie on a circle

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees; the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle; if opposite angles are supplementary the four corners are concyclic; a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to one hundred and eighty degrees, and the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle. The converse shows that points are concyclic. A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle. Real problems combine these facts with triangles, straight lines, the same segment property and the semicircle property.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Reason (1 mark each):** write "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral" or "exterior angle" beside the step
**Working (1–2 marks):** the subtraction from $180^\circ$, or the equation in $x$
**Proof questions:** state the converse you use, then conclude "concyclic"
**Mistake:** pairing adjacent angles instead of opposite angles
**Mistake:** taking the exterior angle equal to the **adjacent** interior angle
**Habit:** check that every opposite pair adds up to $180^\circ$

For a proof, state the converse you use and conclude that the points are concyclic. Common slips are pairing adjacent angles instead of opposite ones, and equating the exterior angle with the adjacent interior angle.

notes.title: Circles: Angle and Cyclic Properties — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Words about a circle
sections.body_md:
- A **chord** joins two points of a circle; a chord through the centre is a **diameter**.
- A chord cuts the circle into a **minor arc** and a **major arc**; the two regions it cuts off are **segments**.
- An arc **subtends** an angle at a point when its two ends are joined to that point.
- Angles are measured at the **centre** (the central angle) or at a point of the **circumference** (an inscribed angle).

*Example:* a chord $PQ$ with $\angle POQ = 80^\circ$ at the centre; the major arc is on the far side of the centre.

key_terms.definition_md: A line segment joining two points of a circle.
An arc or chord subtends an angle at a point when its ends are joined to that point.
The region of a circle cut off by a chord.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O. A diameter AB passes through O, a chord PQ lies above it near the top, and a radius OR runs from O to the lower right of the circle.
visual.caption: Diameter $AB$, chord $PQ$ and radius $OR$. The chord $PQ$ cuts the circle into a minor arc and a major arc.

sections.heading: 2. Angle at the centre and at the circumference
sections.body_md:
- **Theorem:** the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is **double** the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle: $\angle AOB = 2\angle ACB$. The proof joins $PO$ to $Q$ and uses the exterior angles of two isosceles triangles.
- For a point on the **minor** arc, use the reflex angle at the centre: $\angle AQB = \dfrac{1}{2}(360^\circ - \angle AOB)$. Points on opposite sides of a chord see it under supplementary angles.
- Then use $OA = OB$ to find the base angles of $\triangle OAB$.

*Example:* $\angle ACB = 38^\circ$ gives $\angle AOB = 76^\circ$ and $\angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 76^\circ}{2} = 52^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: An angle larger than $180^\circ$; the central angle of the major arc is $360^\circ - \angle AOB$.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O, an arc AB at the bottom subtending 80 degrees at the centre, and a point C on the major arc from which the same arc subtends 40 degrees.
visual.caption: $\angle AOB = 80^\circ = 2 \times \angle ACB = 2 \times 40^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A circle with centre O and a point P at the top. The line PO is produced to meet the circle again at Q at the bottom. A and B are points on either side, joined to O and to P. The angle OPA is marked x with one arc and the angle OPB is marked y with two arcs.
visuals.caption: Join $PO$ and produce it to $Q$. Then $\angle AOQ = 2x$ and $\angle BOQ = 2y$, so $\angle AOB = 2(x + y)$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1: a circle with centre O. The angle AOB at the centre is 110 degrees and the angle ACB at a point C on the major arc is to be found.
visuals.caption: Given $\angle AOB = 110^\circ$; find $\angle ACB$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2: a circle with centre O. A point P on the major arc sees the chord AB under an angle of 38 degrees. The angle AOB at the centre and the base angle OAB of the triangle OAB are marked with question marks.
visuals.caption: Given $\angle APB = 38^\circ$; find $\angle AOB$ and then $\angle OAB$.

visuals.alt: A circle with centre O. The chord AB near the bottom subtends 100 degrees at the centre. A point Q on the minor arc AB, between A and B, sees the chord under 130 degrees, half of the reflex angle 260 degrees.
visuals.caption: From $Q$ on the minor arc the angle is $130^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (360^\circ - 100^\circ)$.

sections.heading: 3. Equal chords and equal arcs
sections.body_md:
- **Equal chords** of a circle subtend **equal angles at the centre**; equal arcs do the same.
- Conversely, equal angles at the centre give equal chords and equal arcs.
- Equal chords (and arcs) also subtend equal angles at the circumference.

*Example:* $AB = BC$ and $\angle AOB = 64^\circ$: $\angle BOC = 64^\circ$, $\angle AOC = 128^\circ$, $\angle ADC = 64^\circ$ for $D$ on the major arc and $\angle ABC = \dfrac{360^\circ - 128^\circ}{2} = 116^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: Chords of the same length; they subtend equal angles at the centre.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and two equal chords AB and CD, marked with one tick each. Each chord is joined to the centre, and the angles AOB and COD at the centre are both 70 degrees.
visual.caption: Equal chords $AB = CD$ subtend equal angles ($70^\circ$) at the centre.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3: a circle with centre O and points A, B and C on the lower part, with equal chords AB and BC marked with ticks. D is a point on the major arc AC. The angle AOB is 64 degrees.
visuals.caption: Chords $AB = BC$, $\angle AOB = 64^\circ$, $D$ on the major arc $AC$.

sections.heading: 4. Angles in the same segment
sections.body_md:
- Angles subtended by the **same chord** at points of the **same side** of it (the same segment) are **equal**: $\angle APB = \angle AQB$.
- Each equals half the angle at the centre on the other side of the chord.
- Points on the **opposite** side of the chord give the supplementary angle.
- Not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus: the proofs that angles in the same segment are equal and of the exterior angle property of a cyclic quadrilateral (section 7). Both results are used.

*Example:* chords $AC$ and $BD$ cut at $E$, $\angle ABD = 58^\circ$ and $\angle DAC = 35^\circ$: $\angle ACD = 58^\circ$, $\angle DBC = 35^\circ$ and $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 58^\circ = 87^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: Points on the same side of a chord lie in the same segment, and see the chord under equal angles.

visual.alt: A circle with a chord AB at the bottom and three points P, Q and R on the upper arc, all on the same side of AB. Each of the three points sees the chord AB under the same angle of 60 degrees.
visual.caption: Angles in the same segment are equal: $\angle APB = \angle AQB = \angle ARB = 60^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4: a circle with four points A, B, C and D in order, joined to form a quadrilateral with both diagonals AC and BD drawn. The angle ABD is marked 58 degrees and the angle DAC is marked 35 degrees.
visuals.caption: Chords $AC$ and $BD$; $\angle ABD = 58^\circ$, $\angle DAC = 35^\circ$.

sections.heading: 5. The angle in a semicircle
sections.body_md:
- The angle in a **semicircle** is a **right angle**: if $AB$ is a diameter and $P$ is on the circle, $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.
- **Proof:** $OA = OP = OB$, so $\angle OAP = \angle OPA = x$ and $\angle OBP = \angle OPB = y$; the angles of $\triangle ABP$ give $2x + 2y = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.
- It is the centre theorem with a central angle of $180^\circ$. A chord that subtends $90^\circ$ at the circumference is a diameter.

*Example:* $\angle CAB = 35^\circ$ in a semicircle gives $\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle at the circumference subtended by a diameter; it is $90^\circ$.

visual.alt: A circle with a horizontal diameter AB through the centre O and a point P on the upper half. The angle APB is marked with a right-angle square. The radius OP is drawn, the angle OAP is marked x and the angle OBP is marked y.
visual.caption: Angle in a semicircle: $x + y + (x + y) = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 5: a circle with diameter AB. A point C above and a point D below the diameter are joined to A and B. The angle CAB is 35 degrees and the angle DBA is 28 degrees; the angles at C and D are marked as right angles.
visuals.caption: Diameter $AB$; $\angle CAB = 35^\circ$, $\angle DBA = 28^\circ$; right angles at $C$ and $D$.

sections.heading: 6. Cyclic quadrilaterals
sections.body_md:
- A quadrilateral is **cyclic** when its four vertices lie on a circle; the vertices are **concyclic**.
- **Theorem:** the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are **supplementary**: $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$ and $\angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ$. The proof joins $B$ and $D$ to the centre: $\angle A = \dfrac{x}{2}$ and $\angle C = \dfrac{360^\circ - x}{2}$.
- A cyclic parallelogram is a **rectangle**; a rectangle and a square are always cyclic; a rhombus is cyclic only if it is a square.
- Algebra: set the sum of opposite angles equal to $180$ and solve.

*Example:* $\angle A = (3x + 5)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (2x - 15)^\circ$ give $5x - 10 = 180$, $x = 38$.

key_terms.definition_md: A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on one circle.
Two angles that add up to $180^\circ$.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The chord BD is joined to the centre. The angle BOD at the centre is 150 degrees, the angle BAD at A is 75 degrees, half of it, and the angle BCD at C is 105 degrees, half of the reflex angle 210 degrees.
visual.caption: $\angle BAD = \dfrac{1}{2}(150^\circ) = 75^\circ$ and $\angle BCD = \dfrac{1}{2}(360^\circ - 150^\circ) = 105^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD with all four corners on a circle. The angles at A and C are 75 degrees and 105 degrees, and the angles at B and D are 78 degrees and 102 degrees. Each pair of opposite angles adds up to 180 degrees.
visuals.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$: $75^\circ + 105^\circ = 180^\circ$ and $78^\circ + 102^\circ = 180^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD drawn inside it so that all four corners A, B, C and D lie on the circle.
visuals.caption: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral: its vertices are concyclic.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The angle at A is 102 degrees and the angle at B is 85 degrees; the angles at C and D are marked with question marks.
visuals.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$ with $\angle DAB = 102^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 85^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The angle at A is marked 3x plus 5 degrees, the angle at C is marked 2x minus 15 degrees, the angle at B is marked 2x plus 9 degrees, and the angle at D is marked with a question mark.
visuals.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$ with $\angle A = (3x + 5)^\circ$, $\angle B = (2x + 9)^\circ$, $\angle C = (2x - 15)^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with both diagonals drawn. The angle ADB is marked 40 degrees and the angle BAC is marked 62 degrees.
visuals.caption: Cyclic $ABCD$; $\angle ADB = 40^\circ$, $\angle BAC = 62^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 6: a circle with diameter AB and a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD above it, with the diagonal AC drawn. The angle ABC is 60 degrees, the angle CAD is 35 degrees, and the angle ACB is marked as a right angle.
visuals.caption: Diameter $AB$; $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$, $\angle CAD = 35^\circ$.

sections.heading: 7. Exterior angle and concyclic points
sections.body_md:
- The **exterior angle** of a cyclic quadrilateral (a side produced) equals the **interior opposite angle**: $\angle DCE = \angle BAD$.
- Use the exterior angle property to find angles without first finding the interior angle.
- **Converse:** if a pair of opposite angles is supplementary, or an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle, the four points are **concyclic**; equal angles on the same side of a chord also give concyclic points.
- When sides $AB$ and $DC$ are produced to meet at $E$, the triangle $EBC$ gives the angle at $E$.

*Example:* $\angle ADC = 70^\circ$ and $\angle DAB = 75^\circ$: $\angle EBC = 70^\circ$, $\angle ECB = 75^\circ$ and $\angle BEC = 180^\circ - 70^\circ - 75^\circ = 35^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle between a side of a polygon and the extension of the next side; for a cyclic quadrilateral it equals the interior opposite angle.
Points that lie on one circle.

visual.alt: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with the side BC produced beyond C to a point E. The exterior angle DCE and the opposite interior angle BAD both carry one arc and measure 75 degrees.
visual.caption: Exterior angle $\angle DCE = 75^\circ$ = interior opposite angle $\angle BAD = 75^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with BC produced to E. The exterior angle DCE is 74 degrees and the angle ABC is 84 degrees; the angles BAD and ADC are marked with question marks.
visuals.caption: Exterior angle $\angle DCE = 74^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 84^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD with a circle through its four corners. The angles at B and D are 88 degrees and 92 degrees, which add up to 180 degrees, so the corners lie on one circle.
visuals.caption: If $\angle B + \angle D = 88^\circ + 92^\circ = 180^\circ$, the four corners lie on a circle.

visuals.alt: Table for worked example 5: the quadrilateral with angles 82, 95, 98 and 85 degrees has both pairs of opposite angles adding to 180 degrees, so it is cyclic; the rhombus with angles 70 and 110 degrees has opposite angles 70 and 70 adding to 140 degrees, so it is not cyclic.
visuals.caption: Test each pair of opposite angles.

visuals.alt: A rectangle ABCD inscribed in a circle. Its diagonals AC and BD are both diameters and cross at the centre O. All four angles of the rectangle are marked as right angles.
visuals.caption: A parallelogram inscribed in a circle is a rectangle; its diagonals are diameters.

visuals.alt: Worked example 7: a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD whose sides AB and DC are produced beyond B and C to meet at a point E. The angle ADC is marked 70 degrees and the angle DAB is marked 75 degrees.
visuals.caption: Sides $AB$ and $DC$ produced meet at $E$; $\angle ADC = 70^\circ$, $\angle DAB = 75^\circ$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Angle-chasing question (3–4 marks):* each angle with its reason 1 mark; correct calculation 1 mark; final answer in degrees 1 mark.
- *Proof of a theorem (3–4 marks):* construction (join $PO$ and produce, or join to the centre) 1; equal radii or exterior angle 1–2; conclusion 1.
- *Algebra with angles (3–4 marks):* property stated 1; equation 1; solution 1; angles found 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually $3 + 3 + 4$; give the reason beside every angle.

**Common mistakes**
1. Halving when the angle at the centre is needed, or doubling when the angle at the circumference is needed.
2. Using the same-segment rule for points on opposite sides of the chord (the angles are then supplementary).
3. Forgetting the reflex angle for a point on the minor arc.
4. Pairing adjacent angles of a cyclic quadrilateral instead of opposite angles.
5. Taking the exterior angle equal to the adjacent interior angle instead of the interior opposite angle.
6. Giving an angle without a reason in a "give reasons" question.

cards.front_md: What is a **chord**, and what is a **diameter**?
cards.back_md: A chord joins two points of a circle; a diameter is a chord through the centre.

cards.front_md: What does it mean that an arc **subtends** an angle at a point?
cards.back_md: The two ends of the arc are joined to that point and the angle between those lines is measured.

cards.front_md: State the **centre and circumference** theorem.
cards.back_md: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle: $\angle AOB = 2\angle ACB$.

cards.front_md: $\angle AOB = 110^\circ$. Find the angle at a point $C$ on the major arc.
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 110^\circ = 55^\circ$.

cards.front_md: $\angle APB = 38^\circ$ at the rim. Find $\angle OAB$.
cards.back_md: $\angle AOB = 76^\circ$, and $OA = OB$, so $\angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 76^\circ}{2} = 52^\circ$.

cards.front_md: How do you find the angle at a point on the **minor** arc?
cards.back_md: Use half of the reflex angle at the centre: $\dfrac{360^\circ - \angle AOB}{2}$.

cards.front_md: A chord subtends $100^\circ$ at the centre. What angle does it subtend on the minor arc?
What do **equal chords** subtend at the centre?
cards.back_md: Equal angles at the centre; equal arcs do the same.

cards.front_md: Two chords are equal and one subtends $64^\circ$ at the centre. What does the other subtend?
cards.back_md: $64^\circ$ as well.

cards.front_md: Common slip with the centre theorem?
cards.back_md: Halving when you should double (or the reverse): the larger angle is always the one at the centre.

cards.front_md: State the **same segment** property.
cards.back_md: Angles subtended by a chord at points on the same side of it are equal: $\angle APB = \angle AQB$.

cards.front_md: A chord subtends $47^\circ$ at a point $K$. What does it subtend at another point $L$ on the same side?
cards.back_md: $47^\circ$, since they are in the same segment.

cards.front_md: What do points on **opposite** sides of a chord see?
cards.back_md: Supplementary angles: they add up to $180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: State the **angle in a semicircle** property.
cards.back_md: If $AB$ is a diameter and $P$ is on the circle, $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Give the proof of the angle in a semicircle.
cards.back_md: $OA = OP = OB$ gives base angles $x$ and $y$; $2x + 2y = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: $AB$ is a diameter and $\angle CAB = 35^\circ$. Find $\angle ABC$.
cards.back_md: $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, so $\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$.

cards.front_md: A chord subtends $90^\circ$ at the circumference. What can you say about it?
cards.back_md: It is a diameter.

cards.front_md: Chords $AC$, $BD$ cross; $\angle ABD = 58^\circ$. Which other angle equals it?
cards.back_md: $\angle ACD = 58^\circ$ (same segment of the chord $AD$).

cards.front_md: What is a **cyclic quadrilateral**?
cards.back_md: A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on one circle (the vertices are concyclic).

cards.front_md: State the opposite angle property of a cyclic quadrilateral.
cards.back_md: Opposite angles are supplementary: $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$ and $\angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: In a cyclic quadrilateral $\angle B = 78^\circ$. Find $\angle D$.
Give the idea of the proof of the opposite angle property.
cards.back_md: Join $B$ and $D$ to the centre: $\angle A = \dfrac{x}{2}$ and $\angle C = \dfrac{360^\circ - x}{2}$, which add to $180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: State the **exterior angle** property.
cards.back_md: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle: $\angle DCE = \angle BAD$.

cards.front_md: $\angle DCE = 85^\circ$ at an extended side. Find $\angle BAD$.
cards.back_md: $\angle BAD = 85^\circ$.

cards.front_md: What is the **converse** of the opposite angle property?
cards.back_md: If a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary, the four vertices are concyclic.

cards.front_md: Is a rhombus with angles $70^\circ$ and $110^\circ$ cyclic?
cards.back_md: No: opposite angles $70^\circ + 70^\circ = 140^\circ \ne 180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: What is a parallelogram inscribed in a circle?
cards.back_md: A rectangle: opposite angles are equal and supplementary, so each is $90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Opposite angles $(3x + 5)^\circ$ and $(2x - 15)^\circ$. Find $x$.
Which equal angles show that four points are concyclic?

questions.stem_md: A chord $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ is viewed from a point $P$ on the major arc. How does the angle $\angle AOB$ at the centre compare with the angle $\angle APB$ at the circumference?
questions.solution_md: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point of the remaining part of the circle. So $\angle AOB = 2 \times \angle APB$. The angles would be equal only for points in the same segment as each other, never the centre and the circumference.

questions.stem_md: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ of a circle with centre $O$ are placed so that $C$ lies on the major arc $AB$ and $\angle ACB = 34^\circ$. The angle $\angle AOB$ measures
questions.solution_md: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc: $2 \times 34^\circ = 68^\circ$. Option (c) halves the angle, (d) treats the two angles as equal and (a) is $180^\circ - 34^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The arc $AB$ of a circular running track subtends $140^\circ$ at the centre $O$. A runner standing at a point $P$ on the major arc looks at the two ends of the arc. The angle $\angle APB$ she sees is
questions.solution_md: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre on the same arc: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 140^\circ = 70^\circ$. Option (d) repeats the central angle, (a) doubles it and (b) is $180^\circ - 140^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $P$ and $Q$ are points of a circle with centre $O$ and $\angle POQ = 96^\circ$. A point $R$ lies on the minor arc $PQ$. Then $\angle PRQ$ equals
questions.solution_md: $R$ is on the minor arc, so the arc it looks at is the major arc, whose angle at the centre is the reflex angle $360^\circ - 96^\circ$. Then $\dfrac{360^\circ - 96^\circ}{2} = 132^\circ$. Option (a) is the angle on the major arc, (b) is the central angle and (c) is $180^\circ - 96^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a circle with centre $O$ the chords $AB$ and $CD$ have the same length, and $\angle AOB = 62^\circ$. The angle $\angle COD$ is
questions.solution_md: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre, so $\angle COD = \angle AOB = 62^\circ$. Option (b) halves it, (c) doubles it and (d) is $180^\circ - 62^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is another point of the circle. If $\angle CAB = 28^\circ$, the angle $\angle ABC$ is
questions.solution_md: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$. In $\triangle ABC$: $180^\circ - 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ$. Option (c) repeats $\angle CAB$, (d) is $\angle ACB$ and (a) is $180^\circ - 28^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Two cameras $K$ and $L$ are fixed on the same arc of a circular rail, on one side of the line joining two statues $M$ and $N$ that stand on the rail. Camera $K$ sees the statues under an angle $\angle MKN = 47^\circ$. The angle $\angle MLN$ seen by camera $L$ is
questions.solution_md: $K$ and $L$ lie in the same segment of the chord $MN$, and angles in the same segment are equal: $\angle MLN = \angle MKN = 47^\circ$. Option (d) doubles it, (a) is $180^\circ - 47^\circ$, which is the angle from the other side of the chord, and (b) halves it.

questions.stem_md: The chords $AC$ and $BD$ of a circle meet at $E$ inside the circle, with $\angle DBC = 35^\circ$ and $\angle AEB = 110^\circ$. The angle $\angle ADB$ is
questions.solution_md: $\angle AEB$ is an exterior angle of $\triangle EBC$, so $\angle ECB = \angle AEB - \angle EBC$: $110^\circ - 35^\circ = 75^\circ$. Then $\angle ADB = \angle ACB = 75^\circ$, as $C$ and $D$ lie in the same segment of the chord $AB$. Option (a) is $\angle DBC$, (b) is $\angle AEB$ and (c) is $180^\circ - 75^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a quadrilateral $PQRS$ whose four vertices lie on one circle, every pair of opposite angles is
questions.solution_md: In a cyclic quadrilateral the opposite angles are supplementary. They are equal only in special cases such as a rectangle, and they add to $90^\circ$ never, since the four angles add to $360^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle and $\angle ABC = 78^\circ$. Then $\angle ADC$ is
questions.solution_md: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$: $180^\circ - 78^\circ = 102^\circ$. Option (c) repeats $\angle ABC$, (d) is $90^\circ - 78^\circ$ and (a) is $360^\circ - 78^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. The side $BC$ is extended to a point $E$ and $\angle DCE = 85^\circ$. The interior angle $\angle BAD$ equals
questions.solution_md: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle, so $\angle BAD = \angle DCE = 85^\circ$. Option (d) is $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 85^\circ$, (a) doubles and (b) halves the angle.

questions.stem_md: In a cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ the opposite angles are $\angle P = (2x + 10)^\circ$ and $\angle R = (3x - 20)^\circ$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution_md: Opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$: $(2x + 10)^\circ + (3x - 20)^\circ = 180^\circ \Rightarrow 5x - 10 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 38$. Check: $\angle P = 86^\circ$, $\angle R = 94^\circ$. Option (a) makes the angles equal, (b) makes them add to $360^\circ$ and (c) halves the answer.

questions.stem_md: In the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ the angle $\angle BAD$ is twice the angle $\angle BCD$. The measure of $\angle BAD$ is
questions.solution_md: Let $\angle BCD = x$ degrees, so $\angle BAD = 2x$. Opposite angles are supplementary: $x + 2x = 180 \Rightarrow 3x = 180 \Rightarrow x = 60$. Then $\angle BAD = 2 \times 60 = 120$. Option (b) is $\angle BCD$, (c) assumes equal angles and (d) doubles the answer again.

questions.stem_md: A stone mason wants a slab that can be cut so that all four corners lie on one circle, whatever its measurements. Which shape should the slab be?

options.text_md: a kite that is not a rhombus
a rhombus that is not a square
a parallelogram that is not a rectangle

questions.solution_md: A quadrilateral has its vertices on a circle when its opposite angles are supplementary. A rectangle has $90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$ for both pairs. In a rhombus or any parallelogram the opposite angles are equal, so they add to $180^\circ$ only if each is $90^\circ$, which makes it a rectangle. A general kite has unequal opposite angles that do not add to $180^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In the quadrilateral $ABCD$ inscribed in a circle, the side $AB$ is a diameter and $\angle BAC = 25^\circ$. The angle $\angle ADC$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle), so in $\triangle ABC$: $180^\circ - 25^\circ - 90^\circ = 65^\circ$. Then $\angle ADC = 180^\circ - \angle ABC$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral): $180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$. Option (d) is $\angle ABC$, (a) is $\angle BAC$ and (b) is $\angle ACB$.

questions.stem_md: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are points of a circle with centre $O$; $C$ lies on the major arc $AB$ and $\angle OAB = 20^\circ$. The angle $\angle ACB$ is
questions.solution_md: $OA = OB$, so $\angle OBA = 20^\circ$ and $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 20^\circ - 20^\circ = 140^\circ$. The angle at the circumference is half of this: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 140^\circ = 70^\circ$. Option (a) is the central angle, (b) is $\angle OAB$ and (c) halves $70^\circ$ again.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a trapezium inscribed in a circle, with $AB \parallel DC$. If $\angle ADC = 105^\circ$, then $\angle ABC$ is
questions.solution_md: $ABCD$ is cyclic, so the opposite angles $\angle ADC$ and $\angle ABC$ are supplementary: $180^\circ - 105^\circ = 75^\circ$. Option (b) repeats $\angle ADC$, (c) is $90^\circ - 75^\circ$ and (d) is a slip of $10^\circ$ in the subtraction.

questions.stem_md: The sides $AB$ and $DC$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are produced to meet at $E$ beyond $B$ and $C$. If $\angle ADC = 85^\circ$ and $\angle AED = 40^\circ$, then $\angle BCE$ is
questions.solution_md: In $\triangle ADE$: $\angle DAE = 180^\circ - 85^\circ - 40^\circ = 55^\circ$, so $\angle BAD = 55^\circ$. The exterior angle $\angle BCE$ of the cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle $\angle BAD$, so $\angle BCE = 55^\circ$. Option (c) is $\angle AED$, (d) is $\angle ADC$ and (a) is $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 55^\circ$.

R is false: angles in the same segment are equal for every chord, whether or not it is a diameter; in the figure both angles are $60^\circ$ and $AB$ is not a diameter.

questions.stem_md: A semicircular archway has its two feet at $A$ and $B$, the ends of a diameter. A stone at any other point $P$ of the arch sees the two feet at a right angle: $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: True. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: with $OA = OB = OP$, the angles of $\triangle APB$ satisfy $x + y + (x + y) = 180^\circ$, so $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: For an arc $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and a point $C$ on the remaining part of the circle, the angle at the centre $\angle AOB$ is half the angle $\angle ACB$ at the circumference.
questions.solution_md: False. It is the other way round: the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference. In the figure $\angle AOB = 80^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 40^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A cyclic quadrilateral has $\angle A = 95^\circ$ at one vertex, so the angle at the opposite vertex $C$ is $85^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: True. The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so $\angle C = 180^\circ - 95^\circ = 85^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A quadrilateral with angles $85^\circ$, $95^\circ$, $85^\circ$, $95^\circ$ in order can be inscribed in a circle.
questions.solution_md: False. The opposite angles $85^\circ$ and $85^\circ$ add up to $170^\circ$, not $180^\circ$, so the vertices cannot lie on one circle. (A cyclic quadrilateral needs each pair of opposite angles to be supplementary.)

questions.stem_md: Two floodlights $K$ and $L$ stand on a circular wall on opposite sides of the line joining two gates $M$ and $N$. Both lights see the gates under the same angle, so $\angle MKN = \angle MLN$.
questions.solution_md: False. Points on opposite sides of a chord lie in different segments; the angles they see add up to $180^\circ$ (the opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral $MKNL$). In the figure they are $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: If the arcs $AB$ and $CD$ of a circle are equal, the chords $AB$ and $CD$ subtend equal angles at the centre.
questions.solution_md: True. Equal arcs subtend equal angles at the centre, and equal arcs have equal chords: here both arcs are $60^\circ$ and both chords are equal.

questions.stem_md: A diameter $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ subtends an angle of $90^\circ$ at the centre $O$.
questions.solution_md: False. $A$, $O$ and $B$ lie on one straight line, so the angle at the centre is $180^\circ$. It is the angle at a point $P$ of the circumference that is $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A square tile $ABCD$ can always be drawn so that all four of its corners lie on one circle.
questions.solution_md: True. Each pair of opposite angles of a square is $90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$, so the opposite angles are supplementary and the square is cyclic (its circle is centred at the intersection of the diagonals).

questions.stem_md: A diameter $AB$ of a circle subtends an angle of ___ degrees at any other point $C$ of the circle.
questions.solution_md: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the angle is $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: An arc of a ferris-wheel rim subtends $118^\circ$ at the hub. A passenger on the major arc sees the ends of that arc under an angle of ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre: $\dfrac{118^\circ}{2} = 59^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The exterior angle formed when a side of a cyclic quadrilateral is produced is equal to the ___ angle.
questions.solution_md: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle (the angle at the vertex not on that side).

questions.stem_md: A cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ has $\angle PQR = 112^\circ$ and the vertices are named in order round the circle. Then $\angle PSR$ = ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\angle PQR$ and $\angle PSR$ are opposite angles, so $\angle PSR = 180^\circ - 112^\circ = 68^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Arcs $AB$ and $BC$ of a circle with centre $O$ are equal and $\angle AOB = 94^\circ$. Then $\angle BOC$ = ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: Equal arcs subtend equal angles at the centre, so $\angle BOC = \angle AOB = 94^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A rotating lamp $S$ and a signal $T$ stand on the same arc of a circular quay, on one side of a chord $XY$. The lamp sees $XY$ under $65^\circ$, so the signal sees it under ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $S$ and $T$ are in the same segment of the chord $XY$, so the angles they see are equal: $65^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $\angle A = 70^\circ$ and $\angle B = 95^\circ$. Then $\angle D$ = ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\angle D$ is opposite to $\angle B$, so $\angle D = 180^\circ - 95^\circ = 85^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a stained-glass rose window with centre $O$, an inscribed angle $\angle APB$ of $36^\circ$ stands on the arc $AB$. The angle $\angle AOB$ at the centre on that arc is ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference: $2 \times 36^\circ = 72^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The ends of an arc $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ are joined to $O$ and the angle $\angle AOB$ is $146^\circ$. A point $C$ on the major arc is joined to $A$ and $B$. Find $\angle ACB$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre on the same arc: $\angle ACB = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 146^\circ = 73^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $A$ and $B$ lie on a circle with centre $O$, and $\angle AOB = 100^\circ$. Find the angle $\angle AQB$ in degrees for a point $Q$ on the minor arc $AB$.
questions.solution_md: The major arc subtends the reflex angle $360^\circ - 100^\circ$ at the centre, and $Q$ sees it from the other side: $\angle AQB = \dfrac{360^\circ - 100^\circ}{2} = 130^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $AB$ is the diameter of a semicircular window frame and $P$ is a point on the frame with $\angle PAB = 37^\circ$. Find $\angle PBA$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\angle APB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). In $\triangle APB$: $\angle PBA = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 37^\circ = 53^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle ABC = 100^\circ$ and $\angle CAD = 36^\circ$. Find $\angle ABD$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\angle CBD = \angle CAD = 36^\circ$ (angles in the same segment of the chord $CD$). Then $\angle ABD = \angle ABC - \angle CBD$: $100^\circ - 36^\circ = 64^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The angles at the opposite vertices $P$ and $R$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ are $(5x - 10)^\circ$ and $(3x + 30)^\circ$. Find $\angle P$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: Opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$: $(5x - 10)^\circ + (3x + 30)^\circ = 180^\circ \Rightarrow 8x + 20 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 20$. Then $\angle P = 5 \times 20 - 10 = 90$ (and $\angle R = 90^\circ$ too).

questions.stem_md: In the cyclic quadrilateral $WXYZ$ the angle at $W$ is $(3x + 10)^\circ$ and the angle at $Y$ is $(2x + 20)^\circ$. Find $x$.
questions.solution_md: $W$ and $Y$ are opposite vertices, so the angles add to $180^\circ$: $(3x + 10)^\circ + (2x + 20)^\circ = 180^\circ \Rightarrow 5x + 30 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 30$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $AB = AD$. The side $BC$ is produced to $E$ and $\angle DCE = 64^\circ$. Find $\angle ABD$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle: $\angle BAD = \angle DCE = 64^\circ$. In the isosceles $\triangle ABD$ the base angles are equal: $\angle ABD = \dfrac{180^\circ - 64^\circ}{2} = 58^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $O$ is the centre of a circle through the corners $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ of a quadrilateral, and the arc $BCD$ (the arc from $B$ to $D$ through $C$) subtends $150^\circ$ at $O$. Find $\angle BCD$, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\angle BAD$ is half the angle at the centre: $\dfrac{150^\circ}{2} = 75^\circ$. $ABCD$ is cyclic, so $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 75^\circ = 105^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a circular medallion with centre $O$, the chord $PQ$ subtends $80^\circ$ at $O$. Find the angle that $PQ$ subtends at a point $X$ on the major arc and at a point $Y$ on the minor arc.

answer.model_answer_md:
At $X$ (major arc) the angle is half the angle at the centre: $\angle PXQ = \dfrac{80^\circ}{2} = 40^\circ$.

At $Y$ (minor arc) the arc seen is the major arc, with centre angle $360^\circ - 80^\circ$: $\angle PYQ = \dfrac{360^\circ - 80^\circ}{2} = 140^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Halve the centre angle, using the reflex angle for a point on the minor arc.

questions.stem_md: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle with centre $O$ and $P$ is any other point of the circle. Join $OP$ and prove that $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OA = OP = OB$ (radii). So $\triangle OAP$ is isosceles: $\angle OAP = \angle OPA = x$; and $\triangle OBP$ is isosceles: $\angle OBP = \angle OPB = y$.

In $\triangle ABP$ the angles add up to $180^\circ$: $x + y + (x + y) = 180^\circ$, so $2(x + y) = 180^\circ$ and $\angle APB = x + y = 90^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Two isosceles triangles on the radius $OP$ give two pairs of equal angles that add to a half-turn.

questions.stem_md: A metal plate $PQRS$ has the angles $\angle P = 84^\circ$, $\angle Q = 97^\circ$, $\angle R = 96^\circ$ and $\angle S = 83^\circ$. Can a circle be drawn through all four corners? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
The opposite angles are $\angle P + \angle R = 84^\circ + 96^\circ = 180^\circ$ and $\angle Q + \angle S = 97^\circ + 83^\circ = 180^\circ$.

Both pairs of opposite angles are supplementary, so $PQRS$ is a cyclic quadrilateral (converse of the opposite-angles property): yes, a circle passes through $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$.

questions.solution_md: Test whether each pair of opposite angles adds to a half-turn.

questions.stem_md: $PQRS$ is a cyclic quadrilateral whose diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ are drawn. If $\angle QPR = 38^\circ$ and $\angle PRS = 67^\circ$, find $\angle QSR$ and $\angle PQS$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\angle QSR = \angle QPR = 38^\circ$, as angles in the same segment of the chord $QR$.

$\angle PQS = \angle PRS = 67^\circ$, as angles in the same segment of the chord $PS$.

questions.solution_md: Each answer is an angle standing on the same chord as a given angle.

questions.stem_md: The side $QR$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ is produced to a point $T$ and $\angle SRT = 110^\circ$. Find $\angle QPS$ and $\angle QRS$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle: $\angle QPS = \angle SRT = 110^\circ$.

$\angle QRS = 180^\circ - \angle SRT = 180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ$ (angles on a straight line), which agrees with $\angle QPS + \angle QRS = 180^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Use the exterior angle for $\angle QPS$ and the straight line $QRT$ for $\angle QRS$.

questions.stem_md: $A$ and $B$ are points of a circle with centre $O$ and $\angle OBA = 25^\circ$. The point $C$ is on the major arc $AB$ and $D$ is on the minor arc $AB$. Find $\angle AOB$, $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OA = OB$, so $\angle OAB = \angle OBA = 25^\circ$ and $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 25^\circ - 25^\circ = 130^\circ$.

The angle on the major arc is half the angle at the centre: $\angle ACB = \dfrac{130^\circ}{2} = 65^\circ$.

For $D$ on the minor arc the angle is half the reflex angle: $\angle ADB = \dfrac{360^\circ - 130^\circ}{2} = 115^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Find the centre angle from the isosceles triangle, then halve it (or its reflex angle).

questions.stem_md: $XY$ is a diameter of a circular disc, and $Z$ and $W$ are points of the rim on opposite sides of $XY$. If $\angle YXZ = 24^\circ$ and $\angle XYW = 31^\circ$, find $\angle XYZ$ and $\angle ZXW$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\angle XZY = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). In $\triangle XYZ$: $\angle XYZ = 90^\circ - 24^\circ = 66^\circ$.

Likewise $\angle XWY = 90^\circ$, so in $\triangle XYW$: $\angle WXY = 90^\circ - 31^\circ = 59^\circ$.

$Z$ and $W$ are on opposite sides of $XY$, so $\angle ZXW = \angle ZXY + \angle YXW = 24^\circ + 59^\circ = 83^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Both $Z$ and $W$ see the diameter at a right angle; use the angle sum of each right-angled triangle.

questions.stem_md: The angles $\angle A$, $\angle B$, $\angle C$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are in the ratio $2 : 3 : 4$. Find all four angles of the quadrilateral.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the angles be $2k$, $3k$, $4k$ degrees. $A$ and $C$ are opposite angles, so they add to $180^\circ$: $2k + 4k = 180 \Rightarrow 6k = 180 \Rightarrow k = 30$.

$\angle A = 2 \times 30 = 60$, $\angle B = 3 \times 30 = 90$ and $\angle C = 4 \times 30 = 120$.

$B$ and $D$ are also opposite, so $\angle D = 180 - 90 = 90$.

questions.solution_md: Use $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$ to find the unit of the ratio, then $\angle D = 180^\circ - \angle B$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. The side $AB$ is produced to $E$, and $\angle CBE = 82^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = 31^\circ$. Find $\angle ADC$, $\angle BDC$ and $\angle ADB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle: $\angle ADC = \angle CBE = 82^\circ$.

$\angle BDC = \angle BAC = 31^\circ$, as angles in the same segment of the chord $BC$.

$B$ lies on the arc $AC$, so $\angle ADB = \angle ADC - \angle BDC$: $82^\circ - 31^\circ = 51^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: $A$, $B$, $C$ are points of a circle with centre $O$, with chord $AB$ equal to chord $BC$ and $\angle AOB = 76^\circ$. Find $\angle BOC$, $\angle ABC$ and $\angle BCA$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, so $\angle BOC = \angle AOB = 76^\circ$.

The arc $AC$ through $B$ is $76^\circ + 76^\circ = 152^\circ$ at the centre, so $B$ on it sees the reflex angle: $\angle ABC = \dfrac{360^\circ - 152^\circ}{2} = 104^\circ$.

$BA = BC$, so $\angle BCA = \angle BAC$ and $\angle BCA = \dfrac{180^\circ - 104^\circ}{2} = 38^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Equal chords give a second centre angle; then use the reflex angle at $B$ and the isosceles triangle $ABC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $AD$ and $\angle ABD = \angle ACD = 39^\circ$: the chord $AD$ subtends equal angles at $B$ and $C$.

By the converse of the same-segment property, $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are concyclic.

Then $\angle BDC = \angle BAC = 47^\circ$ (angles in the same segment of the chord $BC$).
